title: Vettem vagy megvettem? Buying Something Specific

sections.title: vettem vs. megvettem
sections.content: You already know that the past tense agrees with its object the same way the present tense does: an unspecified object takes the indefinite ending, a specific one (marked by *a*, *az*, a possessive, or a name) takes the definite ending. *vesz* ("to buy") is irregular in the past — both endings attach to the same shortened stem *vett*-. *Vettem* egy kabátot. means "I bought a coat" (some coat, indefinite). *Megvettem* a kabátot. means "I bought the coat" (that one, definite) — and the verb prefix *meg-* from Unit 22 adds the sense of a purchase completed. At (én), indefinite and definite *vettem* are the exact same word, so the ending cannot show whether the object is specific; the object does that (*egy kabátot* vs. *a kabátot*). From (te) onward the endings differ too (*vettél* / *vetted*).

sections.title: Same object, two ways
rows: I bought the gift. (the one we talked about)

items.english: Yesterday I bought a nice coat.

items.spanish: Végül megvettem a kabátot, ami a kirakatban volt.
items.english: In the end I bought the coat that was in the shop window.

items.spanish: Károly megvette a jegyeket a moziba.
items.english: Károly bought the tickets for the movies.

sections.content: *meg-* is not required for a definite object: *Vettem a kabátot.* is also correct. *meg-* adds the idea of a finished, specific purchase, so it is very common with *vesz*.
